flicker.d: Something moves, but barely — I may be the only one who can see it.

partial.d: It moves, clearly less than the other side.

near.d: Close to the other side, or the same.

onsetDate.q: When did the facial weakness start?
onsetDate.help: Your best estimate is fine. If it came on overnight, use the morning you noticed it.

diagnosis.q: What diagnosis have you been given?
diagnosis.help: If you are not sure of the exact name, choose the closest option.

bells.d: Idiopathic facial palsy — no specific cause identified.

ramsay.d: Caused by the varicella zoster virus, usually with a rash.

surgical.d: Facial nerve affected during an operation.

none.t: I have not seen a doctor yet

side.q: Which side of your face is affected?

progression.q: How did the weakness come on?
progression.help: This helps us understand whether the pattern is typical.

sudden.d: Over hours, or I woke up with it.

days.d: It got worse across two or three days, then stopped.

gradual.t: Gradually, and it is still getting worse

recurring.d: A previous episode on the same or the other side.

medical.q: Have you been assessed by a doctor?

steroids.t: Yes, and I was prescribed steroids

noSteroids.t: Yes, but no steroids were prescribed

eyeClosure.q: Can you close the affected eye?
eyeClosure.help: Look in a mirror and close both eyes gently, without forcing.

partial.t: Partly — the lid moves but a clear gap remains

none.t: No, the lid does not move

eyeSymptoms.q: Do you have any of these eye symptoms right now?
eyeSymptoms.help: Select everything that applies. This is the most important question on this page.

eyeCare.q: What are you currently using to protect the eye?

tape.t: Taping the lid closed at night

chamber.t: A moisture chamber or eye shield

moveBrow.q: Try to raise your eyebrows. What happens on the affected side?
moveBrow.help: Hold the unaffected eyebrow still with two fingers so it cannot do the work.

moveEye.q: Try to close the affected eye tightly. How much does it move?

moveMouth.q: Try a small smile with your lips together. What happens on the affected side?

synkinesis.q: When you smile, does the affected eye narrow or close on its own?
synkinesis.help: Or the reverse: when you close the eye, does the corner of the mouth pull? Either counts.

tightness.q: Does the affected side of your face feel tight or stiff?

none.t: No, it feels loose or normal

mild.t: A little tight, mostly by the end of the day

moderate.t: Noticeably tight most of the time

severe.t: Very tight — it limits how much I can move

otherSymptoms.q: Do you have any of these?

rash.t: A rash or blisters near the ear, in the ear, or on the scalp

hearing.t: Hearing loss or new sound sensitivity

limb.t: Weakness or numbness in an arm or leg

impact.q: Which of these are difficult right now?
impact.help: This shapes which parts of the daily routine we put in front of you first.

eating.t: Eating — food collects in the cheek

treatment.q: Are you doing any of these already?

perDay.q: How many sessions a day suits your life?
perDay.help: Two shorter sessions works better than one long one, but one done consistently beats two abandoned.

limb.title: Call emergency services now
limb.body: Facial weakness together with weakness or numbness in an arm or leg can be a stroke. This needs emergency assessment, not a rehabilitation programme. Please stop here and call your local emergency number.

eye.title: See a doctor about your eye today
eye.body: Eye pain, persistent redness, or changed vision with facial paralysis can mean the cornea is being damaged by exposure. This is the one complication that can cause lasting harm and it is treatable. Please get it looked at today — an optometrist, GP, or eye casualty department.

rash.title: The rash should be assessed
rash.body: A rash or blisters near the ear alongside facial paralysis suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which is treated with antivirals and has a different course from Bell's palsy. Getting the right diagnosis changes the treatment, so please see a doctor.

undiagnosed.title: You need a diagnosis before you start
undiagnosed.body: Palsya is a rehabilitation programme, not a diagnostic service. Facial weakness has several causes, some of them urgent, and some are treated with medication that works best in the first few days. Please see a doctor first.

progressive.title: Gradual, ongoing worsening needs investigation
progressive.body: Bell's palsy comes on over hours to a few days and then stops getting worse. Weakness that is still progressing over weeks can point to a different cause that needs imaging. Please tell your doctor specifically that it is still worsening.

bilateral.title: Both-sided weakness needs specialist assessment
bilateral.body: Facial weakness on both sides is uncommon and is more often linked to a systemic cause — Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, sarcoidosis, among others. This should be investigated before you begin a rehabilitation programme.

tooEarly.title: It is very early — medical treatment comes first
tooEarly.body:
You are {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} from onset. Corticosteroids started within the first 72 hours measurably improve outcomes in Bell's palsy, and that window matters more right now than starting exercises. Nothing you do with the muscle in the first week changes the nerve.

Come back from day 5. We will hold your answers.

late.title: Outside our usual window — a clinician will review
late.body: Your onset was {days, number} days ago, beyond the 5–90 day window our programme is designed around. Structured rehabilitation still helps at this point, particularly for synkinesis and tightness, but the starting point needs a person to set it. A clinician will review your assessment within one working day before your programme begins.

noEyeCare.title: Start eye protection today
noEyeCare.body: Your eye does not close fully and you are not using anything to protect it. Preservative-free lubricating drops are available without prescription and should start today, with ointment at night. This matters more than any exercise in your programme.

estim.title: About the electrical stimulation
estim.body: We do not include electrical stimulation. The evidence is inconsistent and there is a theoretical concern that stimulation during reinnervation may worsen synkinesis. If a clinician prescribed it for you specifically, follow their advice — but please raise it on your first consultation.

gum.title: Please stop the chewing gum
gum.body: Chewing gum as facial exercise trains the jaw muscles rather than the facial muscles, and it reliably increases tightness and synkinesis. It is one of the few things we would ask you to stop outright.

reasons.noMovement: No voluntary movement in any region, so the programme starts with protection rather than activation.
reasons.minimalMovement: Early voluntary movement is present but minimal, so the work is finding and repeating the smallest accurate movement.
reasons.notIsolated: Movement is present across most of the face but not yet isolated, which puts coordination at the centre of your programme.
reasons.nearNormal: Movement is close to normal in most regions, so the work moves to control at everyday effort levels.
reasons.synkinesisRaised: You described frequent linked movement. Coordination work is the priority when synkinesis is established, even where movement is still limited.
reasons.synkinesisHeldBack: Movement quality would suggest a later stage, but frequent synkinesis is best addressed with coordination work first.
reasons.severeTightness: Severe tightness limits range more than weakness does, so release and coordination work take priority.
reasons.eyeProtection: Because the eyelid does not move, eye protection stays at the front of your daily routine regardless of stage.
reasons.maintenance: More than nine months from onset with near-normal movement and little linked movement — the work now is maintaining range rather than building it.
reasons.slowRecovery: Recovery after {cause, select, ramsay {Ramsay Hunt syndrome} surgical {surgery} other {injury}} is typically slower and less even than after Bell's palsy, so we will not read a slow start as a poor sign.
reasons.timeHoldBack: Your answers alone would suggest Stage {suggested}, but at {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} from onset we hold back a stage. Advancing ahead of the nerve is how compensations get established.
reasons.timeEarliest: At {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} from onset, Stage {stage} is the earliest placement that makes clinical sense.
reasons.clinicianOverride: Your clinician updated your stage after reviewing your progress.

reviewWhy.lowConfidence: some of your answers do not sit together in the usual pattern
reviewWhy.lateOnset: your onset is outside our usual window
reviewWhy.surgeryOrInjury: recovery after surgery or injury needs an individual starting point
reviewWhy.otherDiagnosis: your diagnosis is outside the ones we place automatically
